cctv.faq.3: My CCTV files are .ps — will this work?
cctv.faq.4: Yes. Most Chinese DVRs (Xiongmai, HiSilicon and white-label rebrands) wrap MPEG‐PS in a proprietary header starting with the bytes IMKH. CCTV Converter detects that signature and converts to MP4 with no quality loss in seconds.
cctv.faq.5: What about Dahua .dav or Hikvision files?
cctv.faq.6: Dahua DHAV files convert directly. Hikvision is more varied — standard H.264 backups work fine; encrypted backups (.crypt) can't be decrypted by CCTV Converter and need Hikvision's own player.
cctv.faq.7: Does it really keep all the original quality?
cctv.faq.8: Yes. The default conversion is a stream copy, meaning the video and audio packets are repackaged into MP4 without being decoded or re-encoded. The picture quality is the same as the source. Re-encoding only happens as a fallback if the original stream is incompatible with MP4, and it uses high-quality H.264.
cctv.faq.9: Can I burn the date and time into the video?
cctv.faq.10: Yes — tick “Add timestamp overlay to converted video” in the Convert options menu before you convert. A date/time clock taken from each file’s recording time is burned into the bottom-left of the MP4, incrementing per frame. (See our Terms on relying on output as a sole legal record.)
cctv.faq.11: Can I edit or trim clips?
cctv.faq.12: Yes. Select a file and click Edit… under the preview. The built-in editor lets you trim to the exact frame, crop, rotate, and adjust brightness, contrast, saturation, sharpness and gamma, apply one-tap look presets, reduce night-time grain, and set the output resolution and quality. You can save your settings as presets, automatically blur, pixelate or black out faces, and draw a box over any area — a number plate, a person, an object — that the app then tracks for you. Edits always export to a new MP4 — your original files are never modified.
cctv.faq.13: Can I watch several cameras at once?
cctv.faq.14: Yes — tick the files and choose Multi View from the Tools menu. The Multi-Camera view plays up to six recordings side by side on a single timeline, with per-camera offset nudging so you can line up clocks that have drifted apart. Snapshot every angle at once, build a contact sheet, or export a synchronized composite video.
cctv.faq.15: How do the motion highlights work?
cctv.faq.16: Tick your footage and choose Extract motion highlights… from the Tools menu (or a day's ⋯ menu). The app scans for movement, then exports just the clips where something happens — with adjustable sensitivity and pre/post-roll padding so you keep the run-up and run-out of each event. Save each event separately or as one combined highlight reel, and skip hours of an empty driveway.
cctv.faq.18: Usually many times faster than realtime for a typical CCTV bitrate: a 30-second clip often converts in under a second. With parallel conversion enabled (up to 16 files at once), a full day of recordings — a few hundred clips — can take under a minute on a typical laptop. Optional GPU acceleration (NVIDIA / Intel / AMD) speeds up re-encodes. You can stop at any time; converting again picks up the files that aren't done yet.
cctv.faq.19: What languages is it available in?
cctv.faq.20: 16 languages: English, Indonesian (Bahasa Indonesia), Vietnamese (Tiếng Việt), Thai, Filipino, Chinese (Simplified), Japanese, Korean, Spanish, Portuguese (Brazil), French, German, Russian, Turkish, Ukrainian and Arabic (right-to-left). The app auto-detects your Windows language on first launch and you can switch any time from the globe icon in the toolbar.
cctv.faq.22: Yes. CCTV Converter does its work entirely on your machine and never uploads your footage. Once installed you can disconnect from the internet and it keeps working — the only network use is a quick check for a newer version when the app starts (or when you ask), and if you're offline the check is simply skipped.
cctv.faq.24: Windows 10 or Windows 11, x64. The Microsoft Store version is self-contained — it bundles the .NET runtime and ffmpeg, so there are no prerequisites to install and no admin rights are needed for normal use.
cctv.faq.28: How do I hand footage to someone else, such as an insurer?
cctv.faq.29: Open the clip in the editor and choose Evidence package from the Export menu. You get one folder with a checked copy of the original recording, the MP4 as edited, a report listing what was changed, SHA-256 checksums and a README. If you only need the details and checksums, Evidence report creates a page that opens in any browser and can be printed to PDF. (See our Terms on relying on output as a sole legal record.)
cctv.faq.30: Can I send a clip on WhatsApp?
cctv.faq.31: Yes. In the editor, choose For phone / WhatsApp from the Export menu to save a small copy (16 MB or less) that plays on phones and can be sent in a chat. Compress for email makes a copy of 25 MB or less.
cctv.faq.32: My raw .264 file plays too fast or too slow — why?
cctv.faq.33: Raw .264 and .265 files don't always store how fast they were recorded. CCTV Converter works it out from the recording times in the file names where it can. If a file still plays at the wrong speed, open its ⋯ menu, set the camera's frame rate under Recorded at, and the app offers to convert it again.

cctv.help.15: Install from the Microsoft Store and launch the app. Then:
cctv.help.16: Open your footage — drag a recorder folder (or your DVR's SD card), or some video files, onto the window, or click Choose folder… or Choose files…. The app walks any date subfolders and lists every video file it finds. Once footage is open, the Source folder box at the top lets you switch to another folder.
cctv.help.17: Pick an output folder — where converted MP4s are written. It must be a different folder from your recordings, so your originals are never overwritten. Your recent source and output folders are remembered for next time.
cctv.help.18: Filter and tick — narrow the list with the search box and the duration, date and time filters, then click Tick matching (Reset clears the filters). Files that don't match are hidden and unticked, so only the files you can see get converted. The Tick: links above the list tick All or Unconverted files or Clear the ticks, and each day has its own tick box.
cctv.help.19: Everything runs on your own machine; nothing is uploaded.
cctv.help.21: Tick the files you want and click Convert ticked. Where the source stream is already MP4-compatible the app does a stream copy (no re-encoding, no quality loss, usually very quick); otherwise it re-encodes to clean H.264. Most of the settings below are in the Convert options menu next to the Output folder; the rest say where to find them.
cctv.help.22: Parallel conversion — convert several files at once (up to 16). A day of clips goes much faster on a multi-core PC.
cctv.help.23: Encoder — choose Auto, CPU, or a specific GPU (NVIDIA / Intel / AMD). Auto detects the best available and falls back to CPU if a GPU encode fails.
cctv.help.24: Date/time burn-in — tick "Add timestamp overlay" to burn a per-frame clock into the bottom-left of the output, useful for insurance or incident reports.
cctv.help.25: Merge — from the Tools menu, combine any ticked clips into one continuous MP4 in time order, or right-click a day to merge the whole day.
cctv.help.26: CSV export — from the Tools menu, export the file list (name, size, duration, resolution, format, timestamps) for cataloguing.
cctv.help.27: Optional cleanup — "Delete source files after successful conversion" reclaims space as you go (with confirmation).
cctv.help.29: Select a playable file (a converted MP4, or footage that already plays) and click Edit… under the preview to open the in-place editor. Its settings are arranged in five tabs — Clip, Privacy, Picture, Text & audio and Output — and a gold dot marks any tab you have changed. From there you can:
cctv.help.30: Trim — set the start and end points (down to a single frame) with the range slider or the I/O shortcuts, and mark multiple segments to export separately or merged.
cctv.help.31: Crop & rotate — crop to a region of interest or rotate footage that was recorded sideways.
cctv.help.32: Image adjustments — brightness, contrast, saturation, sharpness and gamma, with a live preview, plus one-tap look presets (Night, Bright, Clarify, Vivid, Black & White) shown as thumbnails.
cctv.help.33: Noise reduction — None / Light / Medium / Strong, to clean up grainy night footage.
cctv.help.34: Output size & quality — pick a resolution and quality level for the exported file. The Output tab shows an estimated file size before you save.
cctv.help.35: Presets — save a combination of edit settings and reapply it in one click.
cctv.help.36: Click Save clip… to write a new MP4 (or use Export ▾ for the other formats below), then Done to go back to your files. Your original files are never modified. A progress bar (with cancel) shows the export as it runs.
cctv.help.38: Tick two to six converted clips and choose Multi View from the Tools menu (or right-click a day) to watch the cameras side by side on a shared timeline. You can:
cctv.help.39: Nudge each camera's sync offset to line up clocks that have drifted apart.
cctv.help.40: Rename and rearrange cells, and solo a cell to hear its audio.
cctv.help.41: Snapshot all cameras at once, or build a combined contact sheet.
cctv.help.42: Export a synchronized composite video of the whole grid; click Stop to cancel an export that is running.
cctv.help.44: Tick footage and choose Extract motion highlights… from the Tools menu (or right-click a file or a day) to have the app scan for movement and keep only the clips where something happens.
cctv.help.45: Sensitivity — Low / Medium / High controls how much movement counts as an event.
cctv.help.46: Pre/post-roll — keep a few seconds before and after each event so nothing is clipped.
cctv.help.47: Output — save each event as its own file, or stitch them all into a single highlight reel.
cctv.help.48: Review — optionally review and deselect false positives before anything is written.
cctv.help.49: Results are cached, so changing the pre/post-roll and re-exporting doesn't repeat the scan.
cctv.help.51: In the preview, Show filmstrip adds a strip of thumbnails above the seek bar for fast scrubbing, and hovering the bar shows a preview pop-up. After a motion scan (Detect motion), a heatmap is painted along the seek bar so you can jump straight to the busy moments; use the prev/next-motion buttons to hop between events.
cctv.help.53: In the Convert options menu, turn on Watch source folder and the app rescans that folder whenever new recordings appear; turn on Auto-convert new files as well and it converts them too — a hands-off workflow for an always-on DVR. It waits until each file has finished being written before converting, and can pop a notification when a batch completes.
cctv.help.57: A few formats are genuinely undecodable by any third-party tool — most notably Hikvision encrypted backups (.crypt), which need Hikvision's own player. Standard Hikvision H.264 backups convert fine.
cctv.help.58: A file won't convert because it's "in use"
cctv.help.59: Another program (Windows' Films & TV, an Explorer preview, or antivirus) may be holding the file. Close any preview windows and try again; the app retries automatically for a few seconds.
cctv.help.60: The preview won't play a source file
cctv.help.61: Some raw CCTV formats can't be previewed until converted. Click Convert & view under the preview to convert the file and play it straight away.
cctv.help.62: Where are my settings and logs?
cctv.help.63: Open About → Open log + cache folder. In the direct-download edition this is %LOCALAPPDATA%\CctvConverter\; the Microsoft Store edition keeps it inside its own app package folder, so the button is the easiest way there. It holds your config, the thumbnail cache and an error log — handy if you ever need to send a support report.
cctv.help.65: Each time it starts, the app checks whether a newer version is available. You can skip an optional update; a required update installs by itself, and the app closes and reopens when it is done. The Microsoft Store edition also updates through the Store. You can choose About → Check for updates at any time. The app makes no other network requests; see the Privacy Policy for details.
cctv.help.66: Still stuck? Email info@davidarthur.app and we'll help.
cctv.help.68: On the editor's Privacy tab, click Detect faces to automatically find and follow faces across the clip, then hide the ones you choose — or click Blur all faces to find and blur every face in one go, then review the boxes. Everything runs on your PC — nothing is uploaded.
cctv.help.69: Detect & track — faces are found and followed as they move, each with a box that tracks it frame by frame.
cctv.help.70: Choose who to hide — click a box to keep that person visible or to redact them; only the faces you pick are hidden.
cctv.help.71: Blackout, pixelate or blur — choose how hidden areas look, and use Box size to grow the face boxes so they cover the whole head.
cctv.help.72: Draw your own & track it — turn on Hide areas manually, drag a box over anything — a number plate, a person, a screen — and click Track this area to make the box follow its subject automatically. Drag a box to move it, or its corner to resize it. If the subject appears at other times too, draw another box there.
cctv.help.73: Automatic detection is a helpful first pass, not a guarantee — always play the clip back and cover anything left exposed before sharing.

cctv.help.81: Right-click a day of recordings (or use its ⋯ menu or the Tools menu) and choose Play as timeline to watch the whole day's files as one continuous video — scrub across the joins, jump to the next motion once motion has been detected in those files, and export any span without opening each file separately.
cctv.help.82: You can also click Detect motion inside the editor to mark active stretches as segments and step between them with the prev/next-motion buttons.
cctv.help.86: Unconverted tab — above the file list, switch from All to Unconverted to hide the files that are already converted, so you only see what is left to do.
cctv.help.87: Raw .264 / .265 files — these don't always store their playback speed. Where it can, the app works it out from the recording times in the file names; if a file still plays too fast or too slow, set the camera's frame rate under ⋯ › Recorded at.
cctv.help.88: Join and split — when recordings carry straight on from each other, a banner offers to join them into one video (the original files are unchanged). A file that holds several cameras shows a Split into … button on its row (also in its ⋯ menu) that makes one video per camera.
cctv.help.89: For phone / WhatsApp — a small copy (16 MB or less) that plays on phones and can be sent in a chat.
cctv.help.90: Evidence package — a folder with a checked copy of the original recording, the MP4 as edited, a report listing what was changed, the checksums and a README.
cctv.help.91: A raw file plays too fast or too slow
cctv.help.92: Raw .264/.265 files don't always store their speed. Open the file's ⋯ menu, set the camera's frame rate under Recorded at, and the app offers to convert it again at the new speed.
cctv.help.93: It says the output folder is the same as the source folder
cctv.help.94: Converting into the folder that holds your recordings could overwrite them, so the app won't do it. Choose a different output folder — a new folder on the same drive is fine.
cctv.help.95: File names — keep the original name, add the date before or after it, or choose Custom… and build a name from {name}, {folder} and {date}.
cctv.help.96: Settings and presets — the Settings button at the top holds the same conversion and watch-folder options, and lets you save them as a named preset to switch between in one click.
cctv.help.97: Speed — make the exported copy play slower or faster (0.5× to 8×), for example to skim a long, quiet stretch.
cctv.help.98: Text & audio — burn the date/time, a label or a watermark into the exported copy, or mute the audio.
cctv.help.99: Pick a Layout (or leave it on Auto), swap two cameras round, and double-click a camera to see it full-window.
cctv.help.100: Snapshot saves the current frame as a JPG (Ctrl+click copies it to the clipboard instead), and Fullscreen (or F) fills the screen.
